title: Troubleshooting
summary: When something about the car behaves differently from usual, learn to identify what's happening, when it happens, and when you must stop.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting method: when to check and when to stop
lessons.summary: Before you identify what's broken, settle one question: is it safe to keep driving?
lessons.body:
# Not guesswork — a process

A car that behaves differently from usual — a new sound, a smell, a warning light, a vibration — doesn't just stay that way for no reason. Something has changed. The safe way to find the cause isn't to guess, but to ask three questions in order: **what exactly is happening, when it happens, and which system in the car is involved**.

## What exactly is happening
Imagine describing the fault to a mechanic on the phone: what kind of sound (a squeal? a knock? a hum?), what colour (smoke, fluid, a warning light), and where on your body you feel it (in the steering wheel, in the pedal, through the whole car).

## When it happens
Under acceleration or braking? In a turn or driving straight? Only when the engine is cold, or also once it has warmed up? At a certain speed, or at every speed? The answer almost always narrows the possibilities down to just a few.

## Which system
Most car faults belong to one of the familiar systems: engine and cooling, brakes and steering, electrical, transmission (gearbox and clutch), tyres and suspension. Once you identify the system, you can go to the matching diagnosis tree in this chapter — for example [[tree:engine-overheating|the engine is overheating]] or [[tree:electrical-fault|an electrical fault]] — and work through it question by question to a diagnosis.

# What you may check yourself, and what belongs to the garage
Some things are safe and simple to check yourself: fluid levels when the engine is cold, tyre air pressure, warning lights that come on at start-up, smells and stains under the car. Other things need tools, lifting the car on a jack, or a [[term:scan-tool|scan tool]] connected to the car — these belong to the garage. Never take apart parts you don't know, and never touch the ignition system, the airbags, or the high-voltage components of an electric vehicle yourself.

# Three severity levels
In every diagnosis tree in this chapter, each diagnosis carries a severity level:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Stop now | Immediate danger — stop in a safe place and do not keep driving |
| Soon | You can reach a garage, but don't put it off for too long |
| OK | You can carry on carefully, following the guidance |

:::danger
Extreme engine heat, smoke, a burning smell, brake failure or loss of steering are always “stop now” — even mid-journey and against your plans. Better to miss an appointment than risk a life.
:::

:::tip Rule of thumb
If you're not sure whether it's safe to keep driving — it isn't. Stop in a safe place and call for help.
:::
keyPoints: Three questions in order: what exactly is happening, when it happens, which system is involved.
You can check fluids, air pressure, warning lights and stains yourself; taking parts apart and computerised diagnosis belong to the garage.
Every diagnosis in the trees carries a severity level: stop now, soon, or OK.
When in doubt, stop in a safe place. Better late than at risk.

lessons.title: Identifying noises: squeals, knocks, hums and more
lessons.summary: Each type of noise points to a different system — learn to listen correctly.
lessons.body:
# The car is talking to you

A new noise is almost always the earliest sign of a fault — before it becomes expensive or dangerous. The first step is identifying the **type** of sound, because each type has different suspects.

# Squealing (a thin, sharp sound)
A steady, harsh squeal when braking is usually [[term:squealing-brakes|squealing brakes]] — a deliberate reminder: the brake pad is almost worn out, and needs replacing soon. A squeal that comes from the front of the car while the engine is running, and changes with engine speed, sometimes points to a [[term:drive-belt|drive belt]] slipping — for example when it's loose or worn.

# Knocking (a short, repeating sound)
A rhythmic metallic knock whose speed rises with engine speed can indicate an internal engine problem — a serious condition that needs an immediate check. A knock from underneath, heard only when you go over a pothole or a speed bump, is closer to the suspension — a worn [[term:shock-absorber|shock absorber]] or a loose part.

# Humming (a low, continuous sound)
A hum that changes with road speed (not with engine speed), and gets stronger when turning in one direction, is a classic sign of a worn [[term:wheel-bearing|wheel bearing]]. A hum that changes with the gear selected is usually linked to the gearbox.

# Knocking in a turn
A rhythmic knock heard only when turning sharply — for example pulling into a parking space — usually points to a worn [[term:cv-joint|CV joint]], especially in front-wheel-drive cars.

# Hissing and whistling
A thin whistle that changes when you press the accelerator pedal, while the car is stationary, may indicate a vacuum leak. A rhythmic blowing or popping noise under the car, even at idle, hints at a leak in the [[term:exhaust-system|exhaust system]] — for example a loosened gasket or pipe.

:::warn
A new noise that doesn't go away within a day or two won't “go away on its own.” In most cases it will only get worse, and more expensive.
:::

The [[tree:strange-noise|new noise]] tree walks you through it question by question, by type of noise, to a diagnosis.
keyPoints: Squealing when braking — usually worn brake pads.
A knock that changes with engine RPM — check the engine immediately.
A hum that changes with road speed and gets stronger in a turn — usually a wheel bearing.
A knock only in a sharp turn — usually a CV joint.
A new noise that doesn't pass within a day or two needs checking, not ignoring.

lessons.title: Smoke and smells: what the colour and the smell tell you
lessons.summary: The colour of the smoke and the source of the smell almost always point to the affected system.
lessons.body:
# Smoke is always a reason to check

A little thin white vapour from the exhaust on a cold morning, which disappears after a minute, is ordinary condensation — not smoke. Any smoke that continues, has a clear colour, or comes from under the bonnet, needs you to stop and check.

# Exhaust smoke by colour

| Colour | Likely source |
|---|---|
| Thick white, sweetens the air | [[term:coolant|coolant]] burning in the combustion chambers — usually a damaged [[term:head-gasket|cylinder head gasket]] |
| Bluish, noticeable on acceleration | [[term:engine-oil|engine oil]] burning — worn piston rings or valve seals |
| Thick black | unburnt excess fuel — usually a clogged [[term:air-filter|air filter]] or an injection fault |

:::danger
Thick white smoke that continues along with rising engine heat is a sign of a damaged head gasket. Continuing to drive can destroy the engine completely. Stop in a safe place and switch off the engine.
:::

# Smoke from other places
Smoke from around a wheel, unrelated to the exhaust pipe, hints at a brake that has seized and overheated (the pad stays pressed against the disc). Smoke from inside the cabin — from the dashboard, from under the seats, or from anywhere that isn't the engine — is **always** urgent: stop, get out of the car, and move away from it.

# Smells
- **A sweet, burnt smell** — coolant leaking onto a hot engine part.
- **A burning smell, like rubber** — a slipping clutch, an overheating brake, or an electrical fault.
- **A strong fuel smell** — a fuel leak. A real fire risk: don't restart the engine, don't light a flame, move away.
- **A rotten-egg smell** — usually a [[term:catalytic-converter|catalytic converter]] working too hard, sometimes because of another engine fault making it overwork.

:::tip
A strong fuel smell inside the cabin, even without smoke, is already a reason to stop and check — don't wait for smoke.
:::

The [[tree:smoke-from-car|smoke from the car]] tree helps you find the source from what you see and smell.
keyPoints: Thin white vapour on a cold morning is ordinary condensation; smoke that continues always needs checking.
Thick white = coolant burning; blue = oil burning; black = excess fuel.
A fuel smell inside the car is a fire risk — stop immediately, don't restart the engine.
Smoke from inside the cabin, not from the engine, is always an emergency.

lessons.title: A fluid stain under the car: what it tells you
lessons.summary: The colour and location of a stain under the car almost always identify the system.
lessons.body:
# Before you panic
A clear stain that collects under the middle of the car on a hot day, after driving with the air conditioning on, is ordinary water from AC condensation. A completely normal occurrence, needing no action.

Any fluid that has colour, feels oily, or has a smell does need attention.

# Location hints at the system

| Location | Main suspect |
|---|---|
| Front, near the [[term:radiator|radiator]] | [[term:coolant|coolant]] |
| Middle of the car, near the gearbox | gearbox oil |
| Near one of the wheels | [[term:brake-fluid|brake fluid]] |
| Near the front of the steering column | [[term:power-steering|power steering]] fluid |
| Anywhere under the engine | [[term:engine-oil|engine oil]] |
| Rear, near the fuel tank | fuel |

# Identifying by colour
- **Green, orange or pink, watery** — coolant.
- **Dark brown to black, oily** — old engine oil or gearbox oil.
- **Red or pinkish, oily** — automatic transmission fluid or power steering fluid.
- **Clear to yellowish, oily, near a wheel** — brake fluid.
- **A sharp fuel smell** — fuel. Do not drive with a fuel leak.

:::danger
A brake fluid stain near a wheel is always “stop now.” The brake system is hydraulic and sealed — a leak means you could lose partial or full braking.
:::

:::tip
Place a sheet of cardboard or white paper under the car overnight and check it in the morning — the stain and its colour show up more clearly than an old mark on asphalt.
:::

For a detailed diagnosis by location and colour — [[tree:leak-under-car|a fluid stain under the car]].
keyPoints: Clear fluid from AC condensation on a hot day is completely normal.
The stain's location (front, middle, near a wheel, rear) points to the suspected system.
Green/orange/pink = cooling; red/pinkish = gearbox or power steering; clear-yellowish near a wheel = brakes.
A brake fluid or fuel leak — don't drive, check immediately.

lessons.title: Vibration and pulling to one side: in the wheel, when braking, or through the whole car
lessons.summary: Where you feel the vibration and when it happens narrows it down to just a few suspects.
lessons.body:
# Where you feel it matters a lot

Vibration in the steering wheel, vibration in the brake pedal, and vibration through the whole driver's seat — three different symptoms, usually with three different causes.

# Vibration in the steering wheel at a certain speed
Vibration that appears at roughly a fixed speed and disappears when you speed up or slow down from it is almost always an unbalanced wheel — it needs [[term:wheel-balancing|wheel balancing]] at a tyre garage. Vibration that gradually worsens with speed, without a particular range, points more to a problem in the drive joints or the wheel itself (a bent rim).

# Vibration in the brake pedal
Vibration or pulsing felt through the brake pedal, mainly when braking from high speed, almost always points to a brake disc that isn't an even thickness — a “warped disc.” It's not immediately dangerous, but it lengthens braking distance and needs attention soon.

# Pulling to one side
A car that consistently pulls to one side, even without braking, on a straight, level road, usually points to incorrect [[term:wheel-alignment|wheel alignment]] — for example after hitting a deep pothole. A difference in tyre air pressure can cause exactly the same feeling, so you always check air pressure first.

# Vibration through the whole car at idle
Vibration felt through the whole car when stationary with the engine running, which disappears once you drive, usually hints at a worn [[term:engine-mount|engine mount]] — a completely different part from the [[term:shock-absorber|shock absorber]], even though the everyday names sound similar.

# Vibration in a turn
Vibration or a knock felt only in a sharp turn, mainly pulling into a parking space, points to a worn [[term:cv-joint|CV joint]].

:::remember
Unequal tyre air pressure is the most common cause of pulling to one side — and also the cheapest to fix. Always check it first.
:::

For a full diagnosis: [[tree:vibration|vibration in the car]] and [[tree:car-pulls-to-side|the car pulls to one side]].
keyPoints: Steering-wheel vibration tied to a certain speed — usually an unbalanced wheel.
Vibration in the brake pedal — usually an uneven brake disc.
Constant pulling to one side — check air pressure first, then wheel alignment.
Vibration through the whole car only at idle — usually a worn engine mount.

lessons.title: Electrical faults: everything, one thing, or flickering
lessons.summary: The scope of the fault — everything, one device, or flickering — points straight to the suspect.
lessons.body:
# The scope of the fault is the first clue

When something electrical stops working, the first question is: is it **everything**, or **one thing**?

# Nothing works
When the headlights are weak, the dashboard lights don't come on, and the radio doesn't respond either — the main suspect is a [[term:flat-battery|flat battery]] or corroded or loose terminals. If the dashboard lights do come on but the starter itself doesn't work, the problem is different (see [[tree:car-wont-start|the car won't start]]).

# Only one device
When only an electric window, the radio, or an interior light stops working, while everything else is fine, the first suspect is a blown [[term:fuse|fuse]] in that circuit. Check the fuse box against the owner's manual: a good fuse looks like an intact metal wire; a blown fuse has a torn or blackened wire. If the fuse is fine but the device still doesn't work, suspicion shifts to a [[term:relay|relay]] or to the switch itself.

# Flickering or dimming
Headlights that dim when you switch on another electrical load (air conditioning, both headlights together), or a battery warning light that comes on while driving, point to the charging system — usually a weak [[term:alternator|alternator]] or a loose drive belt for it. The car is currently “living” off what's left in the battery.

# An intermittent fault
Electrics that cut out for a moment and come back, again and again, usually point to a loose contact in the [[term:wiring-harness|wiring harness]] — for example after water has got in, or a cable has been chafed. This is a stubborn fault to trace, and needs a garage.

:::danger
A burning smell of plastic or rubber, and especially smoke from the dashboard, are a sign of a dangerous electrical fault. Stop, switch off the engine and the electrics, and get out of the car.
:::

:::warn Electric and hybrid vehicles
Never touch the orange cables or the high-voltage components. That's a job for a qualified garage only — even when the car is switched off.
:::

For a step-by-step diagnosis: [[tree:electrical-fault|an electrical fault]] and [[tree:warning-light-on|a warning light has come on]].
keyPoints: Nothing works — usually a flat battery or loose terminals.
Only one device — check the fuse before anything else.
Headlights that dim, or a battery light while driving — the charging system (alternator).
Smoke or a burning smell from the dashboard — stop and get out of the car immediately.
